paragraphs.heading: Same element, different mass
paragraphs.text: Isotopes are different nuclear species, or nuclides, of the same chemical element. All isotopes of one element share an atomic number, the count of protons in the nucleus, so they hold the same position on the periodic table. What differs is the number of neutrons, which changes the mass number, the total of protons and neutrons together. Isotopes of an element have virtually the same chemical properties, but their atomic masses and physical properties differ.

paragraphs.heading: A carbon example
paragraphs.text: Carbon shows the idea clearly. Every carbon atom has 6 protons. Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 therefore carry 6, 7 and 8 neutrons, giving mass numbers of 12, 13 and 14. Of these three, carbon-14 is radioactive, while the other two are stable.

paragraphs.heading: Stable and radioactive
paragraphs.text: Some isotopes are radioactive and are called radioisotopes, while others have never been seen to decay and are called stable isotopes. Earth holds about 339 nuclides that occur naturally. Of those, 286 are primordial, meaning they have been around since the Solar System formed: 251 count as stable, and 35 have half-lives longer than 100 million years. When an element has stable isotopes, those usually make up most of the element found on Earth and in the Solar System.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from Greek roots meaning the same place, because an element's isotopes all sit in one place on the periodic table. Margaret Todd, a Scottish physician, writer and family friend, suggested it in 1913 to the British chemist Frederick Soddy while he was explaining his ideas to her. Soddy then made the term popular.

paragraphs.heading: Soddy's puzzle
paragraphs.text: Soddy first suggested that isotopes exist in 1913. Studies of radioactive decay chains had turned up about 40 different radioactive species between uranium and lead, yet the periodic table had room for only 11 elements over that span, counting lead and uranium. He saw that giving off one alpha particle and then two beta particles produced an element chemically identical to the starting one, but four mass units lighter. So he proposed that several types of atom, differing in their radioactivity, could fill the same place in the table. This work was part of why he received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: Neon splits in two
paragraphs.text: Thomson showed parabolic patches of light on a photographic plate that pointed to two kinds of neon nuclei with different mass-to-charge ratios. He concluded that neon was really a mixture of two gases, with atomic weights of about 20 and about 22. Aston later used a mass spectrograph to find several stable isotopes for many elements. In 1919 he measured neon finely enough to show its two isotopic masses are very close to 20 and 22, while neon gas as a whole has a molar mass of 20.2.

paragraphs.heading: Why atomic weights are not whole
paragraphs.text: This became Aston's whole number rule: when an element's molar mass sits far from a whole number, that is because the element is a mixture of isotopes. In 1920 Aston showed the same for chlorine. Its molar mass of 35.45 is a weighted average of two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, whose masses are almost whole numbers.
